At the core of “
The Kill Team
,” one of 15 films shortlisted for the best documentary Oscar, is a moral dilemma with life-and-death consequences.
On a tour of duty in Afghanistan in 2010, a young American solider, Specialist Adam Winfield, tried to alert superiors when members of his unit began killing civilians for sport. But he was ignored and was soon pressured by his increasingly suspicious squadmates to become an accomplice to the atrocities.
By the time the director Dan Krauss met him, Specialist Winfield was back in the United States,
charged with premeditated murder
and facing a court-martial. Rather than risk his own life by standing up to fellow soldiers, he  remained silent when another killing, meant to be justified with planted weapons, was committed in his presence.
“The film wasn’t intended to be an exculpatory version of the Adam Winfield story,” Mr. Krauss said in an interview in New York last week. But, he added, “when I read about Adam’s story, it had a particular resonance because here was a young guy confronted with a moral crisis, with no clear answer and no clear path out.”
Some of Specialist Winfield’s fellow combatants photographed themselves beside victims posed as if they were trophies, and a few also collected body parts. Mr. Krauss talked to several of those charged along with Specialist Winfield. He also gained access to video footage they shot from their helmet cams, and cuts back and forth between the video and the interviews throughout the film.
Mr. Krauss, 42, was nominated for an Oscar in 2006 for his short “
The Death of Kevin Carter
” and teaches film and television at the
Graduate School of Journalism
at the University of California, Berkeley. During the interview, he talked about both the specifics of making “The Kill Team” and the philosophy of filmmaking he tries to pass on to his students. Here are edited excerpts from that exchange:
Q.
There have always been atrocities in war. What seems new is the ability to harvest video from the main characters and see the war unfolding in real time.
A.
It’s interesting, this temptation for  soldiers to record every part of their experience. It is of course unique to modern warfare, but it’s also part of the impulse to be part of this event in the first place. They want to come home with stories,  pictures. They want to prove to people that they were there,  that they had what it took. You can go on YouTube and find thousands of hours of combat footage.
Q.
For you as a filmmaker, how important a tool is this?
A.
It’s a double-edged sword. You can become inured to this kind of media onslaught. But I think that in instances like this, it becomes an important storytelling tool. Because here you have the very people speaking to us on camera, and they are in the theater of combat. We see them in a different mode, a different psychological mind-state.
Q.
There are people whose whole careers are about war reporting, but you are not one of them. What was it about this particular story that made you take that leap?
A.
I am interested in the moral gray. It’s the human psyche that fascinates me, more than war itself. It just happens that war is an environment in which the human psyche is pushed to its limits. In Adam’s case in particular it was true, because here was a guy accused of acting in the moral wrong and also credited with acting in the moral right.
Q.
This is an eminently journalistic subject, but film is also an art form. How do you resolve the tensions between the two?
A.
I talk a lot to my students about this, because a lot of them, their first impulse is to make art. They want to play with cameras, to make beautiful pictures, and the storytelling sort of falls to the side. There’s always that tension, because you can cover a lot of bad storytelling with beautiful imagery. I don’t work that way: for me the story comes first.
Q.
And where does the artistic component come in?
A.
Part of the beauty of the film is actually in the close-up of the human face. I might be in the minority here. A lot of people talk about talking heads in interviews and films, a term that incenses me. It implies that all “talking heads” have the same value, in other words, none. But these are incredibly engaging young guys, and the way they express themselves, the expressions on their face as they are talking, all communicate so much.
Q.
You’re also very economical. This film comes in under 80 minutes.
A.
Yes, I think a lot of documentaries suffer from being bloated. I almost hesitate to say that, because I don’t want to incur the ire of my fellow filmmakers. But I am a fervent believer in pithiness in storytelling. I think that films deserve to be disciplined and lean. I want to have a tree with its branches pruned, so that we are not veering off in other directions that aren’t advancing the story.
And in the visual aesthetic of the film, I have a similar kind of approach. There is a simplicity or starkness with the imagery, quite intentionally. We wanted a very clean, spare aesthetic; the subject matter demanded a certain restraint and respect.
Q.
About the Oscars — you’ve been through this process before.
A.
Just once, sadly.
Q.
Are you satisfied with the level of interest in this category?
A.
It’s getting more attention than it used to. So that’s encouraging. A lot more people are paying attention to feature documentaries as a filmmaking form, not just as an educational eat-your-vegetables form, but actually as an engaging cinematic experience. You see that with the number of films that are getting into theaters. The artistry of the films is also elevating, so you really get a sense the form is coming into its own.
Q.
What outcome would satisfy you? Is the shortlist enough?
A.
Joking with my friends, I tell them it’s a process of continuously elevating aspirations that are persistently more and more absurd. You start off, “I just want to finish the film,” then you want to get it into the best film festivals, then you want to win the best festivals in the world, then you want to get it nominated for an Oscar, then you want to win the Nobel Peace Prize. There’s just no end to it. I was thrilled to get on the shortlist, and I would love to be able to say that was completely satisfying, that if we don’t get nominated there won’t be a tinge of disappointment. But everyone knows that is preposterous. Everyone who gets this close wants to win. So I’ll say that I’m completely prepared not to get a nomination, and will be completely ecstatic if we do.

To the Editor:
What an uplifting headline: “
On Criminal Justice, the Right and the Left Meet in the Center
” (front page, Feb. 19).
Our leadership in mass incarceration has engaged the entire political system, from those concerned about the huge public costs of our prison population to those concerned about the drug and nonviolent offenders facing a dismal prospect of re-entry.
I hope that prevention will make the list of concerns as well, especially the need to reach young adolescents before they are needlessly arrested or suspended from school for minor misbehavior. They are, after all, our country’s future.
JUDITH S. KAYE
New York
